/SATURDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
Issued at 303 PM MDT Thu Sep 17 2026

This weekend will start out active as SE Wyoming and the Nebraska 
Panhandle will remain under SW flow aloft, which will allow for 
additional surges of monsoonal moisture and chances for 
precipitation. A closed low associated with a rather amplified 
shortwave trough will be located over Idaho and Western Wyoming, 
providing a source for large-scale ascent via DCVA over our area, 
which should set the stage for another round of afternoon/evening 
showers and thunderstorms. PWAT ahead of a closed low will remain at 
or above the 90th percentile for areas east of the I-25 corridor, so 
heavy rainfall will again be a possibility with any storms. Forecast 
soundings across the Nebraska Panhandle on Saturday afternoon and 
evening continue to show tall, skinny CAPE profiles, with warm cloud 
layers near 3 km AGL. This will result in another scenario involving 
efficient warm rain processes (i.e. collision-coalescence) in this 
abnormal, tropical-like air mass that has been in place over the 
past few days. Flash flooding will remain a concern, especially if 
storms manage to train over the same areas that received any heavy 
or excessive rainfall on Thursday or Friday, which we will have more 
specifics on once we see how the heavy rainfall scenario pans out 
today and Friday. Luckily, cloud-layer mean flow remains in the 25-
30 knot range, so any flooding threat would be maximized with any 
training convection, especially as Corfidi upshear and downshear 
vectors are well above 20 knots, so any clusters/lines will be 
propagating at a decent rate.  

There will also be the threat for severe weather on Saturday in the 
Nebraska Panhandle (though likely quite marginal), as deep-layer 
shear is forecast to be around 30-35 knots, especially as we head 
into Saturday evening. With rich low-level moisture with dewpoints 
in the mid to upper-50s and MLCAPE ranging from 1000-1500 J/Kg, 
would not be surprised to see a few supercells capable of producing 
damaging winds and some marginally severe hail (although 700-500 mb 
lapse rates are only ~7 degC/km). Of course, this potential will be 
dependent on how convection evolves on Friday afternoon and 
overnight, which will ultimately determine how much destabilization 
we will see on Saturday during the day. High temperatures Saturday 
will remain in the low to mid-70s east of the I-25 corridor, with 
mid to upper 60s to the west. 

Sunday we will continue to remain active, although most likely less 
so than Saturday, as the closed low translates across our areas and 
transitions into more of an open wave. However, monsoonal moisture 
continues to remain trapped underneath the overall longwave ridge 
pattern. Further, medium-range models are hinting at another weak 
frontal passage sometime Sunday afternoon into the evening, placing 
much of the southern Panhandle in a low-level upslope flow regime. 
This feature, along with the open wave moving across our region, may 
both serve as sources for initiation, although the phasing/placement 
of the two are uncertain at this time. needless to say, heavy rain 
will continue to be a threat, with PWAT remaining between the 70th 
and 80th percentiles. High temperatures on Sunday will be slightly 
cooler than on Saturday, with highs mainly in the upper 60s to low 
70s east of the Laramie Range, and 60s to the west. 

The pattern continues to remain unsettled into the work week, with a 
more zonal flow regime in place downstream of a deep longwave trough 
over California and Nevada. While the westerly flow should result in 
a drier day on Monday relative to this weekend, this open wave will 
slowly move across the Desert Southwest, returning our mid-level 
flow to more southwesterly. Another influx of monsoonal moisture is 
expected sometime early to mid-next week, with NAEFS guidance 
suggesting PWAT anomalies nearing +2 sigma. While not as impressive 
as this most recent moisture surge, can expect daily rounds of 
showers and thunderstorms towards the middle of next week with high 
temperatures at or slightly above seasonal values. Models have been 
inconsistent regarding the timing of a building mid-level ridge over 
the Central United States next week, but can expect an overall 
warming trend through the middle of next week.
